hints: Focus on what ammonia does to alkyl bromides, it replaces each Br with a bond to nitrogen to close a ring.
Count the ring in coniine, it has 5 carbons plus 1 nitrogen in a 6-membered ring with a propyl side chain, so 8 carbons in total.
Imagine opening the ring at the two C-N bonds and putting Br back on those two carbons, how far apart must the two Br atoms be in the open chain?
walkthrough:
**Recognise the reaction type**

Think of this as double nucleophilic substitution. Ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, attacks carbon and displaces bromide.

$$\text{R-Br} + \text{NH}_3 \rightarrow \text{R-NH}_2 + \text{HBr}$$

**See how the ring forms**

Here one $\text{NH}_3$ reacts twice with the same molecule X. The N ends up bonded to two carbons, closing a ring and releasing $2\text{HBr}$.

$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}\text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{coniine} + 2\text{HBr}$$

**Analyse the coniine skeleton**

Coniine is 2-propylpiperidine. The ring contains 5 C atoms plus 1 N atom, and the substituent is $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Total carbons = 5 + 3 = 8, which matches $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}\text{Br}_2$. So X must be an open-chain 8-carbon dibromide.

**Work backwards to place the Br atoms**

Break the two C-N bonds in coniine and put Br back on those two carbons. The N was joined to C1 (a $\text{CH}_2$ in the ring) and to C5 (the $\text{CH}$ bearing the propyl group).

To make a 6-membered ring with N, the two Br atoms must be separated by 4 carbons in the chain. That is $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH(Br)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, which is 1,5-dibromooctane.

options.A: Incorrect. This is a cyclic dibromide, but X must be acyclic with formula C8H16Br2. A cyclopentane plus propyl would be C8H14Br2 after accounting for the ring, so the formula does not fit and no new ring size change occurs.
options.B: Incorrect. Like A, this is already a 5-membered ring. Reaction with ammonia cannot expand it to the 6-membered piperidine ring of coniine, and its formula does not match C8H16Br2.
options.C: Incorrect. 1,4-dibromooctane would join N to C1 and C4. Counting N-C1-C2-C3-C4 gives only a 5-membered ring (a substituted pyrrolidine), not the 6-membered piperidine ring seen in coniine.
options.D: Correct. In 1,5-dibromooctane the Br atoms are on C1 and C5. Linking both to N gives N-C1-C2-C3-C4-C5, a 6-membered ring with the remaining C6-C7-C8 as the propyl group on C5. This is exactly coniine, 2-propylpiperidine.
